posts.title: You learn more about writing from close reading than from writing advice
posts.description: Housekeeping: There will be a reader meetup in SF on December 10: RSVP here. I’ll be in Stockholm on November 26 and made a Luma event if someone wants to meet up . You can also dm me on Substack. If you read writing advice, you’ll often stumble upon all of these rather abstract rules, such as “show, don’t tell,” “open the essay with a concrete story to engage people,” and so on. I don’t find advice like that useful at all. These sorts of maxims remind me of the small notes I might jot down to myself to remember the directions to a friend’s house—“left, right, past the oak tree, right.” Well, that might describe the right way, but it is a very rough map of the terrain, and if it turns out that the person who wrote the notes forgot to mention something—or perhaps was going somewhere other than you—their advice will lead you completely astray. posts.title: Four useful questions
posts.description: Robert Irwin in his Venice, California studio in 1970, photographed by Steve Kahn When I have a problem, Johanna—a.k.a. my wife—typically solves it by asking me one of four questions. 1. Why does it feel bad? If something feels bad, it is useful to articulate very precisely why it feels bad. This helps extract a lot of valuable information. For instance, I was vaguely unhappy with an essay draft I finished today. It just felt ugh. But when I complained to Johanna and she said, “Well, why does it feel bad?” it became obvious to me that the problem was the ending. It is hard to do endings well—they often feel like tying a ribbon on the whole thing; it’s too cute. And this one was a bit like that. “How do you like endings to be?” “I like it when you feel like you are approaching the end, so it’s not abrupt, but at the same time, the ending sort of turns things around.
